title: Nephesh and Decoder Mismatch
compression: Soul can be a usable translation of nephesh, but it can silently import more than the Hebrew source guarantees.
source_reconstruction: Biblical Hebrew nephesh has a broad semantic range involving living beings, life, selfhood, appetite, vitality, and embodied existence. English soul may preserve part of that range while also importing later body-soul assumptions. Recent scholarship also cautions against turning an older monistic correction into a universal rule for every occurrence.
assumption_envelope: One Hebrew lexeme does not by itself establish a complete anthropology.
A traditional translation can remain useful while still carrying decoder risks.
Genesis 2:7 should not be made determinative for every occurrence of nephesh.
Embodied semantics do not automatically settle the monism-versus-separability debate.
decoder_prerequisites: Distinguish translation tradition from lexical identity.
Distinguish embodied semantics from a universal monistic conclusion.
Distinguish source reconstruction from later theological construction.
decompression_map: embodied associations: throat, appetite, breath, vitality
candidate_invariants: No single English gloss exhausts the semantic range of nephesh.
The receiving language can import conceptual assumptions not guaranteed by the source lexeme.
Correcting one decoder bias should not create a new universal overcorrection.
cliffs: Do not reduce nephesh to a detachable modern soul by lexical fiat.
Do not reduce nephesh to a permanently inseparable whole-person concept in every biblical context by lexical fiat.
Do not infer a reader's theology from identity or demographic characteristics.

layers.content: The Hebrew phrase nephesh chayyah is used of living creatures in the waters.
layers.notes: Shows that nephesh terminology is not restricted to uniquely human immaterial identity.

layers.content: The formed human receives the breath of life and becomes a nephesh chayyah.
English versions variously render the result with expressions such as living being, living creature, or living soul.
Scholarly treatments connect nephesh with embodied senses such as throat or neck, appetite, thirst, vitality, life, self, and personhood.
An influential twentieth-century exegetical consensus emphasized psychosomatic unity and often used formulations such as the person is a nephesh rather than merely has one.
layers.source_ref: History of interpretation summarized in Pleijel 2019

layers.content: More recent scholarship has challenged the sufficiency of the older monistic consensus and has renewed attention to contexts in which nephesh may have been perceived as separable from the body.
The English gloss soul may import a modern immaterial and detachable body-soul model that is not established by the Hebrew lexeme alone.
layers.source_ref: Decoder analysis based on lexical and translation scholarship

layers.content: Replacing soul with a rigid rule that nephesh can never be conceived as separable is also stronger than the current scholarly evidence warrants.

A reader may construct a later theological account of soul, embodiment, or afterlife, but Atlas should preserve that account as later construction rather than lexical content automatically contained in nephesh.

decoder_profiles.context: A receiving context in which the English word soul commonly suggests an immaterial personal entity distinct from the body.
likely_assumptions: Soul and body are naturally distinct categories.
Soul language primarily concerns uniquely human interior identity.
A soul can exist apart from bodily life.
The English word soul transparently names the same concept as nephesh.
assumptions_not_guaranteed: That every occurrence of nephesh denotes a detachable immaterial entity.
That the lexical choice alone establishes immortality or postmortem separability.
needed_distinctions: embodied semantic range versus metaphysical conclusion
mismatch_risks: Importing later body-soul dualism into passages where the Hebrew wording does not require it.
Reading Genesis 2:7 as though it simply says a preformed body received a detachable soul.
preparation_notes: Show nonhuman nephesh usage before using soul as a transparent gloss.
Show Genesis 2:7 as a become-a-living-nephesh construction.
Explicitly note the current scholarly debate so decoder preparation does not become a new orthodoxy.
decoder_profiles.status: provisional context profile, not a claim about any individual reader
